title: IBS vs IBD: what separates a functional gut from an inflamed one
summary: IBS vs IBD explained in plain language, including the symptoms that overlap, the warning signs that don't, and the tests that separate them.
body_markdown:
Maybe you’ve been working around your symptoms for months: Cramping after meals, or learning how to stay close to a bathroom whenever you leave your house. Maybe you’ve cancelled plans without saying why.


Somewhere along the way, you started arguing with yourself about whether this is something you can continue to manage or something you need to get checked.


If you want a starting point, Circle Medical offers IBS care with a board-certified provider, often with same-day availability.


## IBS vs IBD at a glance


IBS and IBD aren’t the same condition, even though the names look alike.


IBS is a functional disorder, meaning your bowel behaves abnormally without visible damage.


IBD covers Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis and is driven by inflammation that physically damages the bowel.


- **Core difference:** IBS affects how the bowel works, with no damage to tissue. IBD inflames the bowel and can damage it permanently.
- **Damage:** IBS leaves no visible damage. IBD can cause permanent harm.
- **Warning signs:** Rectal bleeding, unintended weight loss, and symptoms that wake you at night.
- **Test results:** IBS markers are typically normal. IBD often raises calprotectin and CRP.
- **Who manages each:** Primary care for IBS, gastroenterology for IBD.


The CDC estimates[2.4 to 3.1 million Americans live with IBD](https://www.cdc.gov/inflammatory-bowel-disease/php/facts-stats/index.html) .


## IBS vs IBD symptoms: where they overlap and where they split


IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome) and IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease) can share similar symptoms, which is why it’s difficult to identify what you may be going through on your own. Abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, urgency to use the toilet, and fatigue can show up in both conditions.


But IBD is much rarer. Newer studies using Rome IV criteria put IBS at[about 5–6% of people in the U.S.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37595647/)


**IBS (irritable bowel syndrome)** **IBD (inflammatory bowel disease)**


**What it is** A functional disorder of gut-brain interaction A group of lifelong immune-mediated inflammatory diseases


**What drives it** Altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, changes in gut microbiota and nerve signaling An abnormal immune response that inflames the gut


**Bowel damage** None visible on imaging or endoscopy Destructive inflammation that can cause permanent harm


**Core symptoms** Abdominal pain tied to bowel movements, diarrhea, constipation, bloating Persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, urgency


**Symptoms that point toward it** Pain that eases after a bowel movement, symptoms that track with stress or food Rectal bleeding, unintended weight loss, fever, night sweats, anemia


**Blood and stool markers** Typically normal Fecal calprotectin and CRP are often raised


**How it’s diagnosed** Clinically, using Rome IV criteria plus testing to exclude other conditions Objective testing: stool and blood markers, colonoscopy with biopsy, imaging


**How it’s managed** Symptom management, diet approaches discussed with a provider or dietitian, medication when clinically appropriate Medication to control inflammation and hold remission, sometimes surgery


**Who manages it** Primary care, long term Gastroenterology, long term, usually after a primary care referral


Bowel damage is the medical difference between these two conditions, which is why two different specialists can help you manage each of these. If you want to narrow down exactly what you have, the first practical step is a primary care visit.


## What IBS does to the bowel


A scope exam of someone with IBS usually shows healthy tissue. What goes wrong is how the bowel behaves. With IBS, your bowel moves things along too quickly or too slowly, and ordinary bowel stretching can be miscommunicated as pain in your brain.


IBS is diagnosed by criteria instead of scans. Recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least one day per week over the last three months can be a sign of IBS. That pain has to come with at least two of these three: a relationship to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form. Symptoms need to have started at least six months before diagnosis.


### The symptoms come from how the bowel moves and senses


When materials that move through your bowel speed up or slow down, it can change your stool frequency and form. Your gut can report this sensation to your brain as cramping, even if your bowel only goes through regular stretching. That pain can ease after you go to the toilet. If you also experience bloating and urgency to defecate, those fit the same picture of IBS.


However, if you notice blood on your stool, or experience fever and unintended weight loss, you may have a different condition. A bowel with no visible damage doesn’t produce these symptoms.


### What an IBS flare up feels like


An IBS flare up is a stretch of days or weeks when your symptoms can climb above your baseline tolerance. A scope during a flare will show the same intact bowel, just moving and signaling differently. That is why flares come and go without leaving anything behind.


People describe cramping that builds through the day, urgent trips to the bathroom, and bloating that makes their clothes uncomfortable by evening.


IBS triggers vary though stress, poor sleep, hormonal changes, illness, and particular foods.[Low FODMAP eating](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/22466-low-fodmap-diet) is one approach that providers and dietitians use to identify these triggers. This is a conversation to have with a clinician, not a plan to run on your own.


### IBS is not an autoimmune disease


IBS isn’t classified as autoimmune or inflammatory, and nothing about it erodes your tissue. Decades of IBS don’t accumulate into structural harm to your body.


That kind of damage belongs to IBD, where the immune response itself is the problem.


## IBD inflames and scars the digestive tract


The CDC describes[IBD as a group of lifelong diseases affecting the intestines, driven by an abnormal immune response](https://www.cdc.gov/inflammatory-bowel-disease/about/index.html) . The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation states that[IBD can cause destructive inflammation and permanent harm](https://www.crohnscolitisfoundation.org/patientsandcaregivers/what-is-ibd/ibs-vs-ibd) .


Scarring in your bowels is how that harm becomes permanent. In Crohn’s disease, repeated cycles of inflammation and healing can leave scar tissue where normal cells used to be. The narrowing that follows is called a stricture, and[NIDDK lists intestinal obstruction among the complications that can require surgery.](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/crohns-disease/definition-facts)


IBD also runs in waves. Symptoms can flare, settle into remission, and can flare again. The damage it causes can accumulate between cycles, even when someone feels well.


### Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis inflame different parts of the gut


Crohn’s disease can inflame any part of the digestive tract from mouth to anus, often in patches. The inflammation can extend through the full thickness of the bowel wall, narrowing your intestines.


Ulcerative colitis stays in the colon and rectum, where it affects the innermost lining in one continuous stretch. Both conditions are managed by gastroenterology.


### IBD symptoms often reach beyond the digestive tract


Inflammation that is this active doesn’t stay local. IBD symptoms can include persistent diarrhea, abdominal cramping, rectal bleeding and urgency, with weight loss, fever, night sweats, and fatigue alongside it.


The CDC also lists complications outside the gut, including anemia, reduced bone density, joint pain, skin changes, and eye irritation. If your gut symptoms come with joint pain, mouth sores or unexplained anemia, mention all of it at your appointment.


A handful of other symptoms should raise red flags because they don’t fit a functional bowel at all.


## 7 red flags that point away from IBS


Seven symptoms change the question from which condition you have to how soon you need to be seen by a doctor. None of these are typical of IBS, and each is a reason to get assessed instead of waiting it out.


1. **Rectal bleeding or blood in your stool.** Blood isn’t an IBS feature, and it needs a look however well your other symptoms fit.
2. **Weight loss you didn’t intend.** Losing weight without trying suggests something is interfering with absorption or appetite.
3. **Symptoms that wake you from sleep.** IBS rarely pulls people out of bed, so nighttime diarrhea or pain points toward inflammation.
4. **Fever or night sweats.** These are systemic signs, and they point toward an inflammatory or infectious process.
5. **Anemia or persistent fatigue.** A low red blood cell count can signal blood loss or malabsorption.
6. **A family history of IBD or colorectal cancer.** It raises the odds of finding something, and it can change when colorectal cancer screening is recommended for you.
7. **New symptoms starting after age 50.** Bowel symptoms that appear for the first time later in life are less likely to be IBS.


If any of these seven red flags apply to you,[talk to a Circle Medical provider](https://www.circlemedical.com/what-we-treat/ibs) instead of waiting them out.


## How IBS and IBD are diagnosed


The difference between IBS and IBD is clearest in how each diagnosis gets made. IBS is confirmed by matching symptoms against criteria and ruling out a short list of other conditions. IBD is confirmed by finding inflammation through a test.


### IBS diagnosis relies on criteria plus a short list of exclusions


NIDDK notes that in[most cases IBS is diagnosed without tests](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . Any testing that does happen rules other conditions out instead of confirming IBS.


A first round of criteria typically covers a complete blood count, celiac serology, thyroid function and a stool test. Most of it can be ordered as blood work through primary care, drawn at a partner lab near you.


### IBD diagnosis requires objective testing


Symptoms alone can’t confirm IBD. Fecal calprotectin detects a protein white blood cells release into stool, and C-reactive protein does something similar from blood.


When those markers come back raised, the next step is usually a colonoscopy with biopsies, since IBD produces visible inflammation and tissue changes. A colonoscopy can’t detect IBS, because there is nothing structural to find, though a normal result still supports the diagnosis by ruling inflammation out.


Those two paths end in different places, and so does the care that follows.


## Where to go for IBS vs IBD care


Whether for IBS or IBD, your first course of action should be a consultation with a primary care provider. A provider can assess your symptoms, order the first round of testing, diagnose IBS, and manage it long term.


If testing points to IBD, you’ll need to book a consultation with a gastroenterologist. They can walk you through medication that needs ongoing monitoring.

Starting with primary care also keeps other explanations open. Celiac disease, thyroid conditions, reflux, and infection can all produce symptoms people assume are IBS.

## IBS vs IBD FAQs


### Can a colonoscopy detect IBS or IBD?


A colonoscopy can detect IBD. Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis produce visible inflammation and tissue changes a scope can see and a biopsy can confirm. It can’t detect IBS, since IBS creates no structural change to find, though a normal result still supports the diagnosis by ruling inflammation out. The ACG guideline advises against routine colonoscopy under 45 with no warning signs.


### Can IBS turn into IBD?


IBS doesn’t develop into IBD. They’re separate conditions with different mechanisms. What does happen is misdiagnosis. A 2014 UK case-control study found roughly 10% of people eventually diagnosed with IBD had previously been labeled with IBS, and in about 3% the label held for five years or more. If an IBS diagnosis stops fitting, ask for it to be revisited.


### Is IBS an autoimmune disease?


IBS is not an autoimmune disease. Autoimmune conditions involve the immune system attacking the body’s own tissue, which is part of what happens in IBD. IBS is classified as a disorder of gut-brain interaction, where motility, gut sensitivity and nerve signaling behave abnormally. Research has found subtle immune changes in the gut lining of some people with IBS, though not autoimmunity.


### How do you treat an IBS flare up?


Flare management usually involves identifying what sets yours off and adjusting around it, with medication added when clinically appropriate. Providers commonly look at sleep, stress load, recent illness and food triggers, and some use a structured elimination approach such as low FODMAP with dietitian support. If your flares are getting longer or more severe, get reassessed rather than adjusting on your own.


### Can you have IBS and IBD at the same time?


Yes, and more often than most people expect. A 2020 systematic review in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology pooled 27 studies covering 3,169 patients with IBD in remission. It found 32.5% had IBS-type symptoms. For someone whose IBD is controlled, ongoing cramping and loose stools don’t automatically mean inflammation is back. Rechecking markers is how the two get told apart.


### Does IBS increase your risk of bowel cancer?


IBS isn’t known to damage the bowel, and it isn’t considered a risk factor for colorectal cancer. NIDDK describes IBS as producing symptoms without visible signs of damage or disease in the digestive tract. IBS symptoms can still resemble early colorectal cancer, particularly a bowel-habit change that persists, so standard screening still applies based on your age and family history.


### What blood or stool test shows inflammation?


Fecal calprotectin is the stool test most often used. It detects a protein white blood cells release into the bowel, so a raised result suggests intestinal inflammation rather than a functional cause. On the blood side, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate are general inflammatory markers, and a blood count can reveal anemia from blood loss. Providers usually order a combination, since no single result is definitive.
